newsitem.title: USA: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Cautiously bullish ahead of PPI.
newsitem.headline: US CREDIT OUTLOOK - Cautiously bullish ahead of PPI.

text.p: The bullish tone seen on the U.S. credit markets on Friday is likely to spill over into next week, but players should not hold their breath waiting for much lower yields, Wall Street analysts said.

"I would think the generally positive tone that we've seen in the market over this past week will be maintained," said Michael Moran, chief economist at Daiwa Securities America Inc. "(But) I don't think rates will fall much further."
Treasuries rallied sharply last week in anticipation of the release of the September employment report.
The data, released Friday, posted a surprising 40,000 drop in non-farm payrolls against an expected 166,000 rise.
The weak indicator prompted many to believe the Fed will keep interest rates steady in the near future.

A Reuters survey on Friday showed that six of 21 experts projected a possible interest rate hike at the November 13 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, down from more than half of the 32 polled on Monday.
Experts said, however, the underlying trend for the economy is still very blurry.

"The problem is that some in the market are starting to fantasize about a Fed easing. Those guys are on another planet.... This is not the right idea to have yet," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
"This is just one report.... In my mind the risks are still that the economy is going through a pause. But right now the news is on the side of the bulls," Glassman added.
Some of the smoke on the economic scenario will settle on Friday, October 11, with the release of two key economic indicators -- retail sales and the producer price index, both for September.
"I think there is a possibility we might see a high reading on the PPI. That could dent the enthusiasm in the market," Moran said.
"Looking even further out, the consumer price index (due out on October 16) carry high-side risks as well and that could have some influence," he added.

On the retail sales front, pundits said the anecdotal data released so far suggest the number is likely to come on the weak side. The surprise on that indicator, they said, could come from the auto sector, which performed well in September.
From a technical perspective, analysts said the U.S. Treasury market remains in good shape.
Bruce Kamich, senior vice-president and co-manager at MCM MoneyWatch Inc, said he sees a resistance level at 6.72 percent in terms of yields for the U.S. 30-year bellwether.
"It would be nice for those portfolio managers out there that watch these long-term things to see them get close or below 6.72 percent," Kamich said.
"So we're real close to another important buy signal," he added.
The 6-3/4 percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted up 1-8/32 at 100-4/32 in late trading on Friday. Its yield was at 6.74 percent.
The Federal Reserve refrained from open market operations on Friday. Federal funds are seen opening at 5-1/4 percent on Monday, in line with the Fed's target.
The yield curve steepened on Friday, with the spread between the two-year notes and the 30-year bonds widening to 89 basis points in late trading from 84 points on Thursday.
